description:
ElevenLabs turns a written script into spoken audio. It can help creators prepare narration for a video, test different readings of a lesson or make a temporary voice track for an edit. Before signing up through SEOGBTools, ask the team to confirm the access format, usage limits and features included in the offer.

Prepare a script for natural speech

Read the script aloud before generating audio. Put a full stop where the listener needs a pause. Write dates, prices and abbreviations in the form you want spoken. Give unfamiliar names their own pronunciation check. A clean script gives you a better starting point and makes later corrections easier to find.

Generate a short sample

Start with one paragraph that contains the hardest line in the script. Pick a voice suited to the audience and listen at normal speed. Check whether the speaker sounds clear over any music or background noise you intend to use. For a tutorial, prioritize the instructions. For a short story, check whether the pauses and changes in tone support the scene.

Review names, numbers and pacing

Listen while following the script. Mark any word that sounds wrong and regenerate only the affected section where your workflow allows. Compare the revised line with the lines around it so that volume and pace stay consistent. For a multilingual project, have someone who speaks the target language review the names and phrasing.

Export and organize your files

Name each clip by scene and revision so it is easy to find in your editor. Keep the approved script with the corresponding audio files. Play the final edit on headphones and a phone speaker to check that dialogue stays clear. If you are producing a social video, verify captions against the final voice track before posting.

What to check before ordering

Ask which ElevenLabs features and limits are available with this access, including the supported audio formats and whether the intended use is covered. Use voices you have permission to use and check the applicable licensing terms before publishing commercial work. For questions about availability or activation, contact the SEOGBTools team through live chat.

Choose a workflow that fits the project

A voiceover for a short social video has different needs from a course with several lessons. A social clip often needs a strong first line, a clear point and space for a visual beat at the end. A course needs a steady voice and a pace that leaves time to absorb each instruction. A product demo needs narration that matches the timing of the screen recording. Decide which of those problems you are solving before trying voices or adjusting the script. That makes it easier to tell whether the first sample is good enough to build on.

Start with a simple production note. Write down the audience, the language, the intended length and where the audio will appear. Add any words that must be read a particular way. If the voice needs to carry through a series, describe its role in a sentence, such as a calm instructor explaining the next step. Use the note when reviewing samples. A consistent brief helps you compare voices on the work they need to do, rather than on how impressive they sound in isolation.

Write a voice script from the audience’s point of view

Start with what the listener needs to hear. For a tutorial, tell them what they will do and then name the first action. For a story, give them the detail that makes the moment worth listening to. For a product overview, use one example that shows the benefit. Long introductions may work on a written page because readers can skim. In audio, every sentence takes time, so give each line a reason to be there.

Keep the words you want spoken separate from your production notes. If you are working from a video script, make a narration column and a visual column. Put the screen action, the music cue and any camera instruction in the visual column. That gives you clean narration to generate and a clear reference when cutting the video. It also gives a reviewer a way to check whether the words and the images tell the same story.

Consider how the listener will hear the content. They may have one earbud in or be watching while doing something else. Replace a long list of similar steps with a short sentence that names the immediate action. If the next step is important, add a brief pause before it. When a concept needs more explanation, use an example after the definition so the listener can hear how the idea applies.

Test pronunciation before generating the full project

Build a short test script from the hardest parts of the real project. Include one name, one number and one sentence with a natural change in emphasis. For a tutorial, include a label from the interface. For a history video, use a place name and date. For a product video, include the product name and any abbreviation that a listener might misunderstand. This sample gives you better evidence than a generic greeting.

Play it once without looking at the script. Write down what you heard and compare that with what the sentence was supposed to say. This can reveal a word that sounds clear only because you know it is coming. Play it again while following the script and note the exact places where the voice needs attention. Ask another person to listen if a name is central to the topic or if you are working in a language you do not speak.

If the delivery is off, change one thing at a time. Split a long sentence, spell out a number or put a name into a simpler sentence. Then compare the revised sample with the earlier version at a similar volume. Keeping the changes small makes it easier to find the improvement and reuse it. Save a short pronunciation note for names you expect to use in future videos.

Split a long script into useful sections

A chapter, scene or tutorial step is usually a good starting point for a separate clip. Each section should contain a complete idea that can be reviewed on its own. For a documentary, end a section at a transition in time or location. For a course, end it when the learner has completed one task. For a sales video, break after each benefit or demonstration. These boundaries are easier to edit than cuts made at arbitrary word counts.

Keep the voice and reading style consistent across sections. Save an approved sample so you can compare later clips with it. If the opening of a new clip feels too abrupt, listen to it after the previous section and check the spacing between the two. Sometimes the clips are individually fine and the transition simply needs a longer pause. A short review in sequence can save several unnecessary revisions.

Give each clip a name that matches the script. A file called lesson-02-step-03-v2 is easier to place than an export with a generic date. Put approved versions in a separate folder from samples. Keep the raw narration with the final mix so you can adjust captions or background music without rebuilding the voice track from scratch. This matters most when more than one person works on the edit.

Match narration to a video timeline

Put the approved voiceover on the timeline first if it carries the story. Mark the important words and place the relevant visuals near those points. If the voice names a button, show it early enough for viewers to find it. If the voice describes a location, give viewers time to see it before cutting to the next scene. The narration and picture should help the audience follow the same point.

If the video is already cut, review the voice track against the actual timing. Shorten the written sentence if it regularly runs past its visual. Keep the phrase that carries the instruction and remove the part that repeats what viewers can see. Avoid squeezing long sentences into short clips by making every word faster. A few seconds of clear audio are more useful than a crowded explanation.

Listen with the music and sound effects in place. Lower the music during the important lines and check transitions where the sound changes quickly. Test a short export on a phone speaker, where low-level detail can be hard to hear. Then test it with headphones, where clicks and abrupt edits are more noticeable. Both checks can catch problems that are easy to miss while looking at a timeline.

Review captions against the final audio

Generate or edit captions after you approve the narration. A transcript made from an earlier take can keep words that were changed later. Compare captions with the actual track, especially around names, dates and prices. Keep line breaks near natural pauses and allow enough time to read longer terms. Review the caption placement on the device and aspect ratio you plan to publish.

For translated videos, check the meaning in the target language before matching the timing. A literal translation may need more time to say or may sound unnatural. Let a fluent reviewer flag awkward phrasing and double-check names. If a section has to be shorter, preserve the information the audience needs for the next scene. Read the revised line aloud before exporting it.

Build a repeatable checklist for a series

Save the final script, audio files and a short note about what you approved. Include the chosen voice, the pronunciation decisions and any settings you need to reproduce a consistent result. Create a checklist for the next episode. Check the first sentence, verify names and dates, compare the sound with the previous episode and listen to the final export with the captions enabled.

If another editor takes over, send them a sample of a finished episode and a short list of how to name files. Point out which sounds belong to the voice track and which belong to the music or effects. This makes revisions easier and gives the editor a reference when an individual line needs to be replaced. A clear handoff matters more than keeping every unused test clip.

Understand the access offer before signing up

The SEOGBTools signup page is the ordering starting point for this listing. Before committing to a project, ask the support team which access method is provided and which features are included. If you need a particular voice, language, export format or volume of narration, mention it when asking. For a recurring project, estimate the amount of new script you expect each month and allow for revisions, since a first take may need another pass.

Confirm whether you can use the generated audio for the intended project. A private test, a public video and paid client work can have different requirements. Use a voice you have permission to use, and keep any approvals with the project records. Review the relevant platform rules if the video includes synthetic narration that requires disclosure. Ask support about the specific offer instead of assuming every feature or usage right is included.

Frequently asked questions

Is ElevenLabs useful for a first voiceover?

Yes, a short text-to-speech test is a practical way to hear how a script sounds before building the full edit. Use a passage from your own script, not just the simplest opening line. Check whether names and numbers are clear and whether the pace leaves enough time for the visuals. If you already have a narrator, a temporary read can also help you plan timing before the final recording.

What should I do if a word sounds wrong?

Listen to the surrounding sentence and decide if the issue is the word, the sentence structure or the emphasis. Try a simpler sentence or write the term in the way you want it spoken. Regenerate a short section if your workflow allows it. Compare that clip against the previous and next lines before replacing it in the edit.

How do I keep a long narration consistent?

Work in sections, keep one approved audio sample and compare neighboring clips together. Maintain a pronunciation list and label the approved files by scene or chapter. When you make a revision, update the script and the audio filename together so that captions and future edits use the correct version.

How should I check the finished video?

Play the exported file all the way through at normal speed. Check the first line, the loudest scene, any difficult names and the last transition. Turn on captions and look for words that differ from the actual audio. Finally, play a sample on the device your viewers are most likely to use.
